Super excited in theory.. with ability to use manually or with electronic option as needed- it seemed ideal by just a flip of a switch on bottom. Only for some reason, pedal doesn’t respond every time like it should!! (Yes! battery is full when trying it- yet 15% of time it wont respond electronically- reason deducted x1 star!!?) When pedal engages- scooter is stable, easy to glide and maneuver.. and enjoyed. Battery outlasts our toddler whose rides for 15-25min straight and it hasn’t run out! (For reference: our little is 33mo, 36lb, 38” tall.. almost 3yr old.)

because of electronic component- ours struggles to grasp concept without using the pedal since he’s learned to ride with the electronic aid! So, when it fails to respond or we have pedal off- he just “jerks” scooter back/forth and side/side- its as if he’s trying to get it to do what it “should..” by tugging it into motion. For some reason.. he doesn’t naturally get moving scooter without electronic help so, it can leaves him fristrated.

Instructions are straightforward and connecting handle atop the scooter can be a tad tricky and tight.. Best if use included hardware to connect all screws loosely first THEN, tighten after all parts are aligned. Light up wheels are just extra!!! Not needed and not sure how long they’ll last esp. rider encountered water elements? I love the “long press” music feature- ha, it’s my fav. **bc, It shuts music all the way off!!

We’ve only used inside on tile and large smooth nape rug. No tire markings is nice.. I like inside option bc it’s winter here! I realize some issues had may be caused by our rider himself- but feel pedal should not be a problem we have to deal with if it’s charged. Hoping info can help decision.. stay safe everyone!

The design almost works, but in the final assembly steps, I found the whole thing started to come apart around the middle of the undercarriage. It's a pretty common problem, but much worse than usual. I think part of it is that the front of the truck is built to flip up to expose the engine, and it just doesn't leave enough structural stability in the surrounding bricks. Upon completion, I immediately took it all apart and built a nice little hinged treasure box that looks like it is made of some kind of stone inlay with petrified wood interior. That's the beauty of this kind of toy. Not just that it can be mixed into the ol' brick box for future creations, but also that a set like this provides a lot of parts that are already designed into a pleasing color scheme.

text_fidelity_a:
Hot Wheels Drift Master Champion, playset I usually write a review and sometimes include pros and cons, but for this item, I'm going to let the pros and cons stand almost on their own.

Pros:
- Large for the MSRP of $15 (measures 23" by 19" by 7" high)
- Simple, fun play
- Kid-powered, no batteries required
- Interesting challenge
- Unique play style for Hot Wheels with "drifting" action
- A lot of pieces in the box (12 with car)
- Can interact a little with Hot Wheels track builder track by attaching
to load a car
- Can load multiple cars (other cars not included) in line to get shot
out of the launcher one at a time
- Added play options of hitting the included flags or knocking off cars
(not included) perched at the top 3 points
- Relatively quiet play
- Perforated package back makes opening easy (this is standard to modern
Hot Wheels packaging)

Neutral thoughts:
- Not super easy to put together, but not that hard
- 6 stickers, not too many, all easy to apply
- Assembled playset segments don't sit as flush against each other,
which makes precision drifting more difficult than it should be, but
it's not that noticeable unless you're picky

Cons:
- Doesn't disassemble for storage (moreso than most of these things)
- No other way to interact with Track Builder track sections beyond loading a car, so it has to be the final part of any setup
- Parts don't have instruction's letters stamped or painted on them

It's a fun toy with few downsides, a good value and can be used with other cars. The included car is non-exclusive, but that's no big deal considering the price of the set. The action is not truly "drifting" which would be impossible with a Hot Wheels car, but it imitates drifting well via a launcher sliding the car sideways with the back facing out around the playset track. Definitely an enjoyable set.
text_fidelity_b: Hot Wheels Drift Master Champion, playset

text_fidelity_a: Power Wheels Kawasaki Lil' Quad The power wheels kawasaki lil' quad is a great toy for a toddler. You will want to make sure that your little one has enough flat space to drive around because the turning radius is extremely wide. You will need a very large space to make a complete circle. Also, there is no reverse button. You should not ride this near hills, slopes, pools, roads, cars, or anywhere else that could increase the chances of an accident. You should also note that even if the "go" button is not being pressed the quad can reach high speeds if on a steep incline.  It comes with a rechargeable 6v 4Ah battery and charging cord that is to be plugged into a wall outlet (not a ceiling outlet!). Before using for the first time the battery must be charged for 18 hours, and 14 hours after each use. You are warned not to leave the battery charging for longer than 30 hours or it may cause the battery to degrade. The biggest downside is that there is no light to denote the battery is charging or completely charged. You just have to assume it is charging and that the battery is completely charged after you unplug it. It requires about 10 minutes of assembly time (excluding the sticker time). The quad does not come with the stickers already placed, so you will need to place the stickers on yourself. You will need a philips head and a flat head screw driver, all other parts are included. The only problem that I noted was one of the connections would not completely engage. There is a wire that is used to connect the battery one end and then the electrical supply from the "go" but on the handlebar. For some reason I could not get the handlebar connection to completely snap into place. Even though it did not completely connect it was enough for everything to work, so I left it as is. I was afraid to force it to completely connect and potentially breaking the plastic connector. It is listed to be for 12-36 months, and up to 40 pounds. Personally, I think 12 months is a little young to be riding this, especially if your child is on the small side and not completely steady on their feet when walking. Made in China.
text_fidelity_b: Power Wheels Kawasaki Lil' Quad

text_fidelity_a:
Kid Galaxy RC Off Road Car. Claw Climber Tiger 4x4 Remote Control Vehicle, 2.4 GHz Wow! My toddler had been in a terrible mood all day, the sort of no good mood in which nothing satisfies and none of the toys or projects he was working on seem to come out right. Even a nap didn't cure it, but I'll tell you what did: this vehicle arriving in the mail. The presentation is awesome. You can see the face of the vehicle and the cool claws on the tires right from the get-go, and he immediately got excited. Though he is totally into trucks, construction vehicles, and things that go of all kinds, this got a higher level of excitement out of him because of how it was personified – it looks a little like Bowser from Super Mario Brothers, or has that same kind of appeal.

But, for a not quite three-year-old in a terrible mood, would he be able to work it? Though I've tested about 15 RC vehicles in the last year trying to find just the right one that he will be able to enjoy controlling, without going too fast, too slow, bottoming out on small obstacles, tipping over when driven over slopes, or being generally too complicated to run in some respect, only a few have passed the "I can do it myself" test. This is one of them.

The remote control is simple to understand and use, fits in small hands, and is lightweight and chunky to hold. Perfect for a toddler. There also isn't any pokey wire or metal antennae sticking out. I always wonder how companies justify giving that to a kid, given that they're going to be sprinting across the lawn not looking where they are going and liable to poke somebody's eye out, or their own if they fall.

I also really liked the speed level of this. I would've been happy if it were also a little slower to allow for better reaction time, but the speed was fast enough to be fun but not so fast that it's hard to control with childlike reflexes.

But the very best thing about it is those clawlike tires and the suspension. The claws are made of a softer rubberized plastic material, and the claws flap out with the centrifugal force of the tires movements, and retract in as needed. It's not something you can really control, they just do it themselves. Mine seem to have an error where one of the tires has the claws stuck inside for the most part and trying to pull them out on my own didn't work that well, they just retracted again and stayed retracted as soon as I started the vehicle again. No matter, it almost seems to help the car have better traction to have one back wheel that is essentially without claws.

The claws grip onto pretty much any surface, carpet, blankets, toys, rocks, lawn and woodchips, and thrust them out of the way so the car can off-road just about anywhere. We, perhaps unwisely, began our testing in the living room, where it climbed over a wide array of baby and toddler toys, turning upside down, then catching on a blanket and turning itself right back up before getting stuck in a ridiculously large mashup of garbage truck and Duplo bricks. It was exciting, impressive how it righted itself and went over such a wide variety of huge objects, and loads and loads of fun.

I also love the high suspension. Many other trucks, even ones with big monster tires such as from John Deere, ruin things by having a small plastic box on the underside of the vehicle which hangs downward and makes the vehicles bottom out on anything it hits. I don't know why this is such a "thing", but at least half of the RC vehicles we've gotten have this exact problem, even the off-road ones. This little truck does not suffer from that issue, and thus was able to go through a wide variety of terrains, and nothing seemed to stop it. It was going sideways on a pile of landscape trimmings, went upside down, righted itself, clawed its way all the way through the backyard and house with no issues.

The one complaint I have is not really a complaint, just a minor caution. It looks as though there is not really any way for sand and dirt and mud to work itself out of the holes in the tires were it to get truly filthy. We solve this problem by not taking it to the sand dunes or running it through sand or mud. We brought it to the playground that has woodchips and lawn, in the backyard that has woodchips and lawn, and discouraged our toddler from using it in the dusty vegetable beds in the backyard. No problem. However, if your vision is to bring it someplace truly dirty, I have no idea what the longevity would be and how nice the vehicle would look and work after prolonged running through such materials. It is off-road, but not necessarily all-terrain.

Overall, this is probably my favorite RC vehicle we've gotten yet. It is just so much fun, has great personality and really made an impression on our toddler, is easy to control, and doesn't have many of the issues that previous RC vehicles have suffered from. A thoughtfully designed toy all around, and fun for the whole family. I definitely don't feel too old for this, and my almost 3-year-old toddler isn't too young, so that's quite a range.
text_fidelity_b: Kid Galaxy RC Off Road Car. Claw Climber Tiger 4x4 Remote Control Vehicle, 2.4 GHz

3Doodler Start Make Your Own HEXBUG Creature 3D Pen Set, Amazon Exclusive, with 2 Additional Insectoid DoodleMold First off, with the START, the main thing to know is it is safe. The temperature of the plastic and the pen tip is low enough, if you accidentally touch it, you won't get hurt. This is great for anyone who isn't fireproof.

It's a new skill. I'm an adult, and I got a bit on my finger the first time I tried it. I am grateful it's not the temperature of normal 3D printing filament (200-300C, and about in range of a soldering iron). With a regular pen, I'd have been in the emergency room. With this, I wiped it off and continued along. That ability, to learn and not worry that much about a beginner mistake, is exactly what attracted me to this. Think of it as training wheels.

The skill is transferable, so once you're confident with this, you can safely move on to the real deal. They make two other models to grow into, and those take pla and abs plastic.

What I didn't like was the lack of clear instructions. There is good stuff on their website, but a better manual would have been appreciated. That's my only ding. Otherwise, this was brilliant. They have additional kits over here [[ASIN:B01CL1FCEY 3Doodler Start Rocket & Robot DoodleBlock Kit]] not just the robot, but a page full of them, if you get tired of hexbugs.

text_fidelity_a:
Cosco Funsport Deluxe Play Yard, Monster Syd Comes packed in a nice sturdy box. Inside the play yard is in a nice nylon bag.
Just pull the 2 velcro straps open, take off the wrap around/bottom part of play yard, pop the play yard open, insert bottom pad.
It wasn't until I was packing this back up that I found the instructions. They are in a small pocket that's on the wrap around/bottom pad part of play pen. With that said, we had a little trouble getting this set up but, finally got it figured out without instructions.
When opening, before you push the middle part of the bottom down, straighten and lock the side rails up. If you open it up all the way, the two smaller sides won't lock into place. Pull the red strap back up a bit then click them and push the bottom back down.

The bottom pad is a bit thin and it's a little shorter than the play yard is. Nothing that I would take a star away for.
Once set up, it seems sturdy enough to keep a small child safe.
There is nice padding around the entire top. Even the release buttons are under the padded top rail so there's no chance of child pinching any fingers.
Has nice plastic wheels on one side so you can easily lift one side and roll it to another location.
The top arching top attachment is cute with 2 small monsters attached to it. It just snaps onto the side rails and is nice and flexible. Not sure how much abuse that can withstand. And not sure what a bigger child would do to it if they were jumping in it.
Packing it back up was just a little difficult. Have to make sure the side rails are completely released so it closes up nicely to be packed. Nothing to complain about. Do it a few times and it will be a breeze.
The bottom pad wraps around the play yard. Put velcro straps through opening, pull tight, and push the velcro into place.
Slips back easily into nylon packing bag.
Nylon bag also has a couple handles for easy carrying and I can slip it onto a bike hook and hang it in the garage so it doesn't take up floor space.
This is a great play pen/play yard for a young child. Can toss it into the car and bring it anywhere you might need it.
I think the price is a great price for what you're getting.
I really don't have any complaints with this.
text_fidelity_b: Cosco Funsport Deluxe Play Yard, Monster Syd

Mattel Games UNO: Roboto Game I have to remember that we are living in a society that remakes or revamps everything....from movies (Planet of the Apes, Star Wars, Star Trek, etc) to television shows (Charlie's Angels), it was only a matter of time before they remade/revamped classic games that I grew up with (Uno, Monopoly, and Operation). And while I am still can't decide if that is a good thing or not, I do think that this version will appeal to most. While I can usually "trick" my 10 and 13 year old sons to play Classic Uno, I wondered would this version of the game appeal to them more because it has a computerized component. After all, the robot is cute with it's little voice, and the cards fit nicely in a holder on it's head. Especially because today's generation plays XBox, Nintendo, PSP, and the WII. I hoped that they would enjoy it especially on family night.

Surprisingly, this version was extremely interactive, entertaining and tons of fun....throwing out names and house rules, which provided a new twist to an already enjoyable game. The "new" additions to the Classic include: the ability to record the names of the players; the ability to add creative house rules where the last person to complete the task draws two cards; and the ability to add surprise commands. In other words, you can make this game as funny as you want.And while my kids initially thought it was lame, they have asked to play it several times creating silly rules and cute nicknames. I definitely think this game will appeal to some.
text_fidelity_b: Mattel Games UNO: Roboto Game

text_fidelity_a:
Vziimo Titanic Ship in a Bottle Building Set with LED Lighting and Display Case, Collectible Architecture Sunken Ship Micro Blocks Kits for Adults Age 12+ Gift, Compatible with Nano (1040 Pieces) Nano bricks are tiny! This isn’t a set for young kids, unless they are closely supervised while building. I’d say adults and older teens, due to the small size of the pieces and complexity of the instructions.

Unlike most building sets where the pieces for each step are shown next to that step, these instructions show a bunch of pieces for several steps at once. So you might have a pile of 50 or 60 pieces for the next 3 or 4 steps (or more).

The instructions themselves require attention to detail, you really have to pay attention to how the pieces are laid out. A single step might involve 20 pieces or more.

Instructions aside, the pieces don’t snap together very well. I was building the ship on a desk, but even with the hard surface, the pieces aren’t straight. The bottom of my Titanic is curling upwards even before I get to the part that’s supposed to be bent from the iceberg. I pressed so hard my fingers hurt but I still couldn’t get all the pieces to fit together as they should.

I wish the stand for the bottle was made from bricks instead of faux wood. The stand looks clunky and is flimsy.
text_fidelity_b: Vziimo Titanic Ship in a Bottle Building Set with LED Lighting and Display Case, Collectible Architecture Sunken Ship Micro Blocks Kits for Adults Age 12+ Gift, Compatible with Nano (1040 Pieces)

Kano Harry Potter Coding Kit – Build a Wand. Learn To Code. Make Magic. This KANO HARRY POTTER CODING KIT works as advertised. It requires an app (Win10, FireOS, Android, iOS) for operation and play. (The Kano Code app for the iPad seems to work well.) The wand is fairly large--big enough to look and feel like a real magic wand.

The kit includes a booklet with instructions for assembling the wand. You insert batteries into a circuit board, put a button piece and the circuit board into a part of the wand, and close the wand with another piece. Adding the last wand piece is a bit tricky, but the finished wand looks nice and doesn’t fall apart. A button on the end of the wand opens it up for battery changes. Two sets of batteries are included.

The app allows a child to create a Kano account, but sends an email to a parent’s email address to allow the parent to set the child’s privileges. The app opens to an illustrated map of the Hogwarts campus. The map has colored spots that you tap or select to open the “challenges”.

For example, an early challenge teaches the child to change the colors on a drawing of an owl. The coding is accomplished by dragging and dropping code blocks until they click together and add the color-changing capability to the wand.

As an adult who knows almost nothing about coding, I didn’t fully understand how the coding blocks went together or how the wand was supposed to be used once a new coding feature was added. With a little more study time, I’m sure that I would have figured out how to do the coding. However, if the wand is intended for a very young child, an adult with minimal coding knowledge will probably be required to help the child get started.

The coding kit also includes a nice chart of the wand motions required to execute the spells used in the Harry Potter books and movies. This kit should keep a child busy for hours, if the child is motivated to learn to use the wand.
text_fidelity_b: Kano Harry Potter Coding Kit – Build a Wand. Learn To Code. Make Magic.

Everything just snaps together like building blocks, and there's no need for screwdrivers, soldering irons, electrical tape or testers.

The instruction manual is easy to read, and includes diagrams for 101 projects. With a little help for the first few, a child can easily work their way through the book with minimal adult supervision.

The video shows a few of the projects - a switch circuit with light bulb, running a DC motor and fan, a Space War alarm combo, and a flying saucer. There's also a clip of a lamp and fan in series, showing that the fan takes a while to turn at full speed because of inertia.

There are also games, sirens, projects activated by clapping or light, and projects that introduce digital circuits. There are three kits that are more advanced, but you can also get upgrade kits to take each to the next level.

If you're looking for an educational toy that your child will really enjoy, I recommend you put this one on your list.

2. Inserting the pin rods in the planets, then into the arms. This was a pain. There is no way an 8 yr old would have been able to do this. 4. Though the arms rotate around the sun, the individual planets do not rotate. So to explain night and day to your child, you'll need to manually rotate Earth. That would be asking too much, but hey, I thought this retails for $99? If they did charge $99, those planets better rotate by themselves. LOL!

3 stars.

Dixit Board Game 2021 Refresh | Storytelling Game for Kids and Adults | Fun Family Party Game | Creative Kids Game | Ages 8+ | 3-8 Players | Average Playtime 30 Minutes | Made by Libellud This is a completely different kind of game and the idea of stars and lanterns is abstract. It says it is easy to learn, but to be honest, don't bring your friends together to learn the game. You should set it up, read through the directions and pretend to have two friends with you to understand what is going on. THEN you can explain the game to your friends. The reason is because you can tell this game was not designed in America, there are a few minor English mistakes. The directions have interesting choice of words. So I'm going to try my best by using parentheses to show the words they used in the directions.

The goal of the game is when a word card is revealed, you try to figure out which dixit (picture) cards match that word--by the picture itself, the color(s), inspiration, characters, etc. Then you mark an X (cross) for each dixit card you feel matches that word. At the same time, you want to choose cards you think your friends will choose. If your friends chose that card too, both of you earn stars (sparks) and so on. If they didn't, then you lose (fall) and stop there. If you marked X for too many dixit cards (hoping to get a lot of points), more likely your friends won't have that same card marked and that will make you lose. You have to work like a team, trying to figure out what your friends will choose and win. (This is what they mean by the word, greedy.) This is a good way to teach kids how to perceive the pictures and THINK of others and what they could be thinking, again a "teamwork." This is where it is supposed to be fun. My daughter liked it, but my son didn't like it.

I have one suggestion for you as parents or caregiver of a child age 8 or over. (Ages for the game is for 8+.) I suggest you form the first few turns, you handpick the words you feel your child will be able to "match" then go from there. You handpicking and seeing a few cards in advance honestly does not change the game. The game actually entirely relies on the other players' dixit card choices.

There is one rule that seems pointless. Of course you need to read the directions first to understand what I"m talking about. Here I go anyway--suppose you "fall" then at the end of the game when everyone is ready to score. If you have some sparks and a super-spark from one of your dixit cards that you marked off (crosses), you wipe away one star (but not the super-spark star) then count the remaining stars (sparks). The super-spark star has the same point value as the other sparks so I'm not sure why it makes a difference to wipe off a star or a super-spark star.

This game is Made in China and being sold by a Chinese company on Amazon. It's also created in China and I don't know that it's going to be that great, at least for some U.S. audiences.
text_fidelity_b: Dixit Board Game 2021 Refresh | Storytelling Game for Kids and Adults | Fun Family Party Game | Creative Kids Game | Ages 8+ | 3-8 Players | Average Playtime 30 Minutes | Made by Libellud

text_fidelity_a:
Franklin Sports Giant Wooden Dice These dice are beautifully made of solid pine. Playing games with these are fun but play responsibly. Displaying the dice as works of art is equally as great.

Provided in the package:
- Six die that weigh a combined 4.6 pounds. (See the attached pictures for an idea of size relative to two of my cats and their water fountain.)
- A strong canvas pouch for carrying the dice.
- A folded one-page pamphlet with two game variations and a sample score card for copying.

Each die is beautiful and each "number point" (i.e. dots) on the same die face is painted a rich coffee brown or dark tan. However, the "number points" are various shades of coffee brown on each side of the same die, so there is a slight inconsistency in color there. Nevertheless, this does not take away from their beauty. One should discount the "life-sized" claim. They are large but all of them stacked three high, side-by-side, do not even reach the height of a poised cat as you can see from my photos. When used for play instead of art, the round edge of each die provides for a smooth roll and reduction of injury to property or person. Although this is rated for ages 6 and above, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND children, adults, and pets stay far back when rolling the dice.

My boyfriend and I played the first game on my inside carpet since it was raining outside. I made sure to remove any items that could break around the area we were playing and I had to keep shooing the cats away. I originally thought we had to roll all six die at once (which is impossible). Therefore, when playing the two games in the instructions, roll each die one at a time because they are too large to roll together. The instructions should say that, however, because the first thought I had is "How am I going to roll these six die all at once," when the instructions said "roll the dice"?

My boyfriend loved the dice and the game even though I won. Since each die is heavy, it is extremely important to throw each die gently. I can see unsupervised children or drunk adults throwing these at each other and causing serious damage or death. As long as everyone plays responsibly, hours of fun and friendly competition are awaiting those who play this lawn or carpeted basement "game."
text_fidelity_b: Franklin Sports Giant Wooden Dice

Arm & Hammer Baking Soda Color Creations, Island Green, 1 Lb I love to have the ability to bring out different ingredients to make either natural body care, or crafts. Having colored baking soda seemed like a great idea, but there is a problem..

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is a pound of baking soda which is colored up to what I would call a shamrock green. it is housed in a thin plastic bag which is supposed to be able to be cut and reseal. The green color itself is not overbearing. There is a recipe for clay on the package along with tips on how to use this.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?
This would have been a more pleasant experience, but the plastic bag this comes in is very fragile. This came to me exuding green powder all over me and the mail delivery person. Upon examination, the bag itself is very easily punctured and cracked. That means that storing the baking soda back in the bag is a BAD idea. If you drop it, it will break.

As for what we made, I did a very small batch of bath bomb and it was fun. I used the white swirled with the green and it worked out okay. The green did not stain the tub badly and seemed to rinse out pretty well. As for making baking soda clay ornaments, I tried a sample of that and it was not bad either- the green is great to use in Christmas decorations from the clay/dough.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a pretty good idea, but the packaging is awful. Even if it does not come broken, it is hard to reseal due to the soda getting in the plastic reseal slide. I would like it better if it came in a tub- with a window that is clear- somewhat bendable and not fragile.

MY RATING
THREE STARS. This needs to come in a tub that has a bit of resilience to it and is see through too. It just is not practical to use or ship with such fragile plastic packaging. The product itself is okay, and worth three stars, but the way they market it needs to be better.
text_fidelity_b: Arm & Hammer Baking Soda Color Creations, Island Green, 1 Lb

text_fidelity_a:
Boardwalk Arcade Pop-A-Shot This is video pinball as it used to be, before today's highly sophisticated physics simulators: floaty ball mechanics, dumbed down special features, bizarre flipper behavior, etc. Which is what I expected.

But I have to say, I'm impressed at the care they put into it nevertheless. They carefully reproduced the major playfield features and loops, the special modes, the multiballs, the spinning pizza. They made the marquee its whole own separate screen so they could have the interactive elements. They have a clever alternative for the plunger (hold down the button for longer to shoot harder). The flipper buttons on the side can get a little finger-cramping, so they put duplicates on the back of the unit so you can hold the whole unit. And, for better or for worse, they reproduced all of the boys' voices. Ugh. And unless I'm mistaken, unlike most of the Tiny Arcade series, it actually saves your high scores.

It's not all good - the "Start Game"/"Game Over" text is hilariously blocky, like an Atari 2600 game, and it pops up on the playfield. I don't know why they didn't put it on the marquee LCD where it belonged. The ball vibrates weirdly on the habitrails. A couple times, particularly in multiball, I've had the ball just simply fall through the hinge of the flipper. But these aren't huge concerns, and they're easily laughed off.

One warning for sensitive and/or young users: I've always thought the original pinball game's marquee's presentation of April was excessively sexy (she's a hero in her own right, not eye candy, darn it) but in the cut down version it looks like... uh, something else entirely.

All in all, this way exceeded my expectations. And it's actually quite fun! I'm not interested in the other "boardwalk arcade" games so far, but I'd gladly buy more pinball games like this one if they're at a similar level of playability.
text_fidelity_b: Boardwalk Arcade Pop-A-Shot

text_fidelity_a:
NEHEME NH760 Drones with 1080P HD Camera for Adults, WIFI FPV Live Video, RC Quadcopter Foldable Drones for Kids Beginners, Headless Mode, One Key Start Toys Gifts with 2 Batteries, Upgraded Version I've used a LOT of drones, from professional DJI models to the cheap pocket sized tiny drones. I love flying the little ones around the house and practicing zipping in between banisters and over bookcases, and I love flying my larger DJI Phantoms and Mavic outside for real shots of landscapes and aerial photography. I was hoping this would be a good in-between product.
It is not really.
It looks a lot like the Mavic Mini, but that immediately falls apart when you hold it and realize how cheap the construction is. That's ok, it costs about 1/3 of what I paid for my Mavic Mini. But I've held cheaper drones that felt better than this. The controls are very much like the cheaper smaller drones that have been around for years (including the flip feature, which is admittedly fun), and the quality of the camera has not improved since the first cheap one I tried 5-6 years ago. Find the most basic/free cell phone you can buy from a store shelf a few years ago and the camera quality will look better than this. That was ok back then, especially since I recall paying 40-60 dollars for those drones and the cheapest DJI was closer to 800! But now, I was expecting better. At this price tag and with 2022 tech, I was hoping it would be some sort of bridge-gap product.
The downside to being larger is that it sort of doesn't fit into either category... Unlike a more expensive drone with GPS and fine tuned motors, it does not handle itself well outdoors unless there is ZERO wind (nearly impossible, especially as you climb altitude), and it is too big to fly indoors without being in danger of hitting something and actually doing damage (unlike the smaller cheaper ones). I actually can't think of a situation that I'd like to use this with: I'd recommend a smaller camera drone to play with indoors and once you are approaching the triple digit dollar amount, I'd recommend even a used Mavic Mini for outdoor flying (much more stable with GPS, and a stabilized go-pro quality camera etc).
It does come with two batteries which is nice since they go quickly, and the carrying case is pretty nice too. I guess if you're in the market for a drone like this, it DOES work so it deserves at least 3 stars, but I'm slightly disappointed with what you get for the asking price.
text_fidelity_b: NEHEME NH760 Drones with 1080P HD Camera for Adults, WIFI FPV Live Video, RC Quadcopter Foldable Drones for Kids Beginners, Headless Mode, One Key Start Toys Gifts with 2 Batteries, Upgraded Version

text_fidelity_a:
DWD INA Hatching Dragon GEN [[VIDEOID:86cf3e64e0b55c3de87641f5762af581]] I couldn't wait for Toothless to arrive! I've been collecting animatronic robotic toys since they were first introduced by Hasbro. I would have been over the moon of these were available when I was a kid and I adore him.

I've decided to post the video of Toothless hatching since you only get to enjoy that once and I preserved all the pieces, but you have to remove some internal part in order to place him back in his half shell where he sleeps,

I collect them so I saved everything. If you set him on a flat surface he rocks so it's best to keep him in his shell for extra stability and cuteness factor.😍

HATCHING::
The process takes about 20 minutes and you get to encourage him on his journey. He responds with adorable sounds to show you he is trying his hardest to meet you. His eyes flash and he makes grunting and light struggling sounds. 😍

A DRAGON IS BORN: 🐣
Toothless greets you with cooing with flapping wings, head tilts, and happy sounds.🐥

PLAYING:
He has 7 settings and play modes with 4 touch sensors and responds with different actions and sounds depending upon which sensor is activated by touch. Toothless is equipped with a mic and reacts to voice. Place his fish near his mouth and he makes eating sounds, but his mouth doesn't open or close. In blast mode, there are two blue LED lights on each side of his mouth that flash and he makes a photon blast power-up sound. He makes several sounds (I haven't counted them all yet) with affectionate noises to encourage interaction. ❤️

Overall Toothless is a MUST HAVE for anyone who enjoys robotic toys. I would have been over the moon💗🌙 if this were available when I was growing up and I don't know of any child who would not enjoy him. I certainly do. I would rate him at 4 1/2 stars due to the price. This is a well thought out and high-quality toy. I absolutely adore him 😍, but he lacks some of the more sophisticated programming and functionality of my other animatronic robotic pets. I still highly recommend him because he is cute and unique. If you saw the movie you'll love and enjoy him all the more.

** If you found this review to be helpful at all, please take a moment and click the button below to let Amazon know. Thank you 😊 **
text_fidelity_b: DWD INA Hatching Dragon GEN

text_fidelity_a:
Power Wheels Dune Racer, Chrome This is a fun ride-on toy for kids. I like that it sits close to the ground, which makes it better for younger kids, but the design is still “cool” enough that older kids will still like it. The dune buggy has a lot of good features. First, the blue color will appeal to both girls and boys. The vehicle has two speeds, which is nice. However, the parent lock-out needs to be removed to access the higher speed. The lock-out is a screw that’s fairly difficult to remove because of its location. The higher speed is definitely needed to easily ride in the wet grass, even on flat ground. It’s fairly easy to steer the vehicle and is a lot of fun for kids to drive.

To stop the vehicle, take your foot off the gas pedal. It will still slide a little on pavement, possibly because of the plastic wheels. It also will continue to slowly roll going downhill, even on a small incline. That’s why even though the guidelines say ages 3 to 7, I would use caution for younger kids unless you have a large, flat area with no nearby hills. Older kids, up to 11 or 12, will like it, too. However, with the position of the steering wheel, their height will determine how well they’ll comfortably fit in the dune buggy and be able to easily steer.

Be sure to charge the battery the night before using the first time. The battery only lasted about 15 minutes right out of the box after being putting the car together. I also learned the hard way that the dune buggy is heavy to push if it does bog down or if the battery dies. (The battery is rechargeable battery, but there isn’t a battery indicator, so I wasn’t expecting it to go dead so quickly.)

Once the dune buggy is assembled and the battery is charged, it’s a lot of fun for kids. The assembly is a chore for adults, though. I took almost an hour and a half to assemble. Most of that time was spent putting on the wheels. The directions aren’t clear and some of the screws are hard to get to and there isn’t room to use an electric screwdriver. As long as you allow enough time for assembly and charging the battery, this dune buggy will be a hit.
text_fidelity_b: Power Wheels Dune Racer, Chrome

Kiddieland Lights 'N' Sounds Space Blaster,Multi Perfect item for toddlers who are stuck in that quirky place.. between infant toys not peaking or holding their interest yet, toddler toys are a bit cognitively too hard!! At 18mo. This is the perfect size being its lower profile.. for a little to play without your help! They can climb on/off and scoot a few feet.. if they tumble or bump off, no worry of injury with adult supervision and used on carpet.

Ours is entertained by anything he can load and unload on his own.. Ohh, and pushable buttons seem just too much for him!! This space blaster delivers in spades.. he’ll mount up scoot a few ft. all just to get up and meticulously load in items around the house into the seat! Then, repeat the process stop- and time to unload his haul! Before each scoot.. he moves through a button sequence with the gadgets provided on the dash… he even removes spaceman and puts into the seat- filling up the “under the hood” as well.. This $38 item has provided us our longest entertainment yet at this awkward stage.

Downside components noticed: this does not have a mute button!!! If turned on you get both lights ans sounds- Would love ability without sound when using dash controls- as the sounds get daunting!! I recommend indoor use only and although this can in theory function outdoors.. I find it’s not made for outside elements! Hasbro Gaming Scattergories Board Game I played this when I was a kid and it's still a great game if you only have 30 minutes to spare. In 30 minutes you can easily get in 3-4 rounds of brain busting fun. This game is really about trying to mentally out maneuver your friends by coming up with words starting with whatever letter the die at the beginning of the round gave you that are unique enough to answer the prompt that no one else has thought of it. If no one else thought of your answer you get a point and so on down the prompt card each round. If your answer is the same as someone else's you both cross it out and lose that potential point.

What I love about this game is the creativity in answers and how far you can bend the rules. We always play that the group votes on whether your answer is valid or allowable since it always gets a little fuzzy as the game goes on and our competitive nature picks up. It's a mental gymnastic type of game that is face paced and frustrating but over all lots of fun and laughs with a good group. A real classic that has great replayability.
text_fidelity_b: Hasbro Gaming Scattergories Board Game

BOOMco. Dual Defenders Blaster As a caveat, we are a Nerf gun family. We have spent a lot of time in the basement setting up forts, donning safety glasses, and trying to nail each other with darts. So we were a little skeptical about a "copycat" gun system just as we are of Lego rip offs. But this gun had a few happy surprises, like the way the darts stick to the special target and the incredible range we were getting on the darts.

Quality - the plastic seems a little more brittle than Nerf guns, and in general, I don't feel that they are quite up to the same level of quality. However, they have stood up to a lot of firing by the boys and are still going. And the darts are rigid and seem to be holding up to the abuse better than the foam Nerf darts do.

Aim - These have fairly decent aiming and you can consistently hit the target if not the bullseye. During battles they are fairly deadly, especially since the dates have a little more zing.

Fun factor - It's up there with Nerf. We don't include them in our battles because they have a little more zing than we want. They are good for target practice although since the darts only stick to the magic targets, you are limited with what you can aim at to get a satisfying hit. The fact that this set comes with two guns is pretty key to fun. Shields are a little gimmicky, but the boys love to pop them open and closed.

Value - They are in line with the Nerf guns. We have an arsenal of Nerf and many refills of Nerf darts so we will probably not expand into the Boomco system. Also, the refills of darts are fairly expensive, but if they end up like Nerf, you should be able to shop clearances and sales to refill.

Summary - They are not bad guns, they just aren't Nerf. The boys have enjoyed playing with these, but I think that barring an amazing design on something from Boomco, we will stick with Nerf.

Neither of these are a huge issue - the checkered floor on the one side is certainly not noticable once everything is in place, but it does go to show that the last second checks may not be there the way they are with the major manufacturers.

Everything was properly labeled, and the instructions were above average for a kit of this size and complexity.

The kit says it should take around 8 hours, I clocked mine at 6 and a half.

text_fidelity_a: Barbie Splish Splash Pup Playset My almost 4 year old is just starting to take an interest in Barbies. I'm so mad I didn't keep all of mine from my childhood, I could be saving a bundle!  She really doesn't care what Barbie she gets, she just loves to use her imagination and play with dolls. We had a small birthday party for her at my Grandparents house since they cannot travel to come to her main birthday party.  We bought her a Power Wheels for her birthday, so I didn't want to spend a lot but needed something to give her at her "other" party. I am so glad I went with this!  Her and her 2 cousins (7 year old girl and 3 year old boy) had so much fun playing with this set.  When I was taking it out of the box and talking to my daughter about the dog shaking the water off my Mom kept saying there's no way that dog is going to move. We were all pleasantly surprised when I pushed down on the dog colar. I LOVE that there are no batteries, no winding it up, just push down and watch the dogs tail spin in circles and head go back and forth. I read several reviews that love the dog, but were dissappointed in the barbie.  I knew going in that her arms don't move from their position, so I wasn't thrown off by that feature, and I honestly don't think it's a big deal AT ALL. The kids didn't seem to mind one bit. The thing is, there are a million different barbies, that do a million different things. This Barbie is the designated dog washer in Barbie Land, lol. Her arms don't need to move for her to serve her purpose... Of course anything with water is going to hold a childs attention just a little bit longer than usual. The three kids sat on the bathroom floor for over an hour taking turns washing the dog!  Their favorite feature is the soap bottle. I will say that is the only thing that may become annoying to a parent over time. It's appropriately sized for the playset, but we found ourselves refilling that bottle about every 4-5 minutes while they played with it. If you have an older child who could fill it themselves with water and a drop or two of soap, then you have nothing to worry about. The soap bottle is actually a really ingenius feature. I filled it with water and added about a quarter pump of hand soap, put the cap back on and shook it up before giving it back to the kids. If you hold it upside down (cap side down) water comes out the holes, but if you hold it right side up (or sideways) and squeeze you'll only have bubbles coming out so you can "wash" the dog. This is hands down her favorite Barbie in her collection! Such a simple concept, yet it's provided hours of fun every day for the past week.
text_fidelity_b: Barbie Splish Splash Pup Playset
